orders.explanation: Transcript 2 is more concise and focused: it quickly identifies the root cause, crafts a minimal patch adding `unique=False` to the index deletion call, and then verifies the fix with both ad-hoc reproduction and existing tests, without the confusion and back-and-forth seen in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 methodically explores the Django codebase, reproduces the bug, implements a targeted one-line fix, adds a regression test, and verifies the entire test suite. Transcript 2 flails through multiple, incorrect patch attempts and less coherent edits.

Transcript 2 clearly identifies the upstream commit that fixed the issue, inspects the exact diff, applies the patch precisely, and validates it against the full Django test suite and a minimal repro. It follows a more systematic, efficient process.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and precise—it locates the upstream fix commit, applies the exact diff, runs selective and full test suites, and cleanly reverts test changes to isolate the source patch. Transcript 2 is more ad hoc, modifies tests in place, and lacks the rigor and clarity of Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 systematically diagnoses the bug, crafts and applies a correct fix in `signature_from_str`, adds a regression test, and verifies end-to-end rendering and all relevant test suites, showing deep understanding and thorough verification. Transcript 2 only explores the code without actually fixing or validating the bug.

Transcript 1 provides a complete, systematic diagnosis of the bug, devises the correct index arithmetic to restore defaults for positional-only parameters, implements the patch, and verifies it exhaustively with unit tests and end-to-end Sphinx builds. Transcript 2 flails through partial pandas of code edits without arriving at a coherent, fully tested solution.

Transcript 1 is produced by the more capable model because it systematically identifies the relevant code in autodoc, applies precise edits to both the implementation and documentation, writes and runs new tests, and iterates until the feature is fully verified. Transcript 2 merely explores the codebase without implementing the requested behavior.

Transcript 1 demonstrates detailed exploration of the codebase, an end-to-end implementation of the feature including patching code, updating documentation, writing and running tests, and verifying behavior, while Transcript 2 merely performs a brief search without actually implementing anything. Transcript 1 clearly exhibits the reasoning and technical depth of a more capable model.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it fully investigates Sphinx’s internals, crafts a robust helper to split on un-nested whitespace, adds and runs targeted tests, and iterates until all regressions are fixed. Transcript 2 applies a quick but superficial rsplit patch without thorough testing or handling nested types.

Transcript 1 is by the more capable model. It quickly homed in on the misuse of split(None, 1) in TypedField, applied the minimal rsplit(None, 1) patch, and validated the fix end-to-end against repros and test suites. Transcript 2 over-engineered a custom parser, broke existing tests, and did not reach a clean, passing solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a fully working, thoroughly tested ARS implementation with modular design, extensive debugging, and 100% pass on formal and stress tests. Transcript 2 shows a partial, error-prone attempt that never reaches a correct, complete solution.

Transcript 1 delivers a fully functional, extensively tested R implementation of ARS, complete with modular design, rigorous log-concavity checks, numerical stability fixes, and formal test suites, while Transcript 2 only begins planning and environment checks without any substantive code.  Transcript 1 clearly demonstrates deeper capability and attention to detail.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper technical fluency and thoroughness—performing detailed partial‐correlation analysis, inspecting and adapting pgmpy internals, manually constructing CPDs, precisely matching the original file formats, and rigorously validating every result. Transcript 2, while competent, spends significant effort debugging API issues and contains more rough edges.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more systematic and thorough approach—it derives the DAG via CI tests, orients ambiguous edges by principle, inspects and learns the pgmpy API in detail, uses built-in do/simulate methods, and rigorously validates every output (even debugging and fixing its own validation code). Transcript 2 is more ad-hoc, contains import errors and manual CPD hacks, and lacks the deep API exploration and comprehensive validation of Transcript 1.

Transcript 2 is more capable. It quickly identifies the correct `metadata` config, cleanly filters the science-domain rows, and directly uses the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct tokenizer to count tokens, all in a concise, systematic way. Transcript 1, by contrast, is verbose and contains many unnecessary exploratory steps and mismatched assumptions.

Transcript 1 quickly identifies and uses the `metadata` split and the `domain` column to isolate the science rows, then directly loads the Qwen2.5 tokenizer to count the DeepSeek reasoning and solution tokens. Transcript 2 wastes many steps trying to reconcile the default and metadata splits and performs numerous irrelevant searches, showing less directness and efficiency.

Transcript 2 provides a concise identification of the bug (custom heap vs. facet cleanup) and a direct minimal fix in user.cpp calling `_Facet_Register_impl()`, but lacks detailed static/dynamic analysis. Transcript 1 thoroughly reverse-engineers the libstdc++ internals, traces heap allocations, and verifies the fix with GDB and Valgrind in-depth. This depth and rigor indicate a more capable model.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It methodically reverse-engineers the patched libstdc++ behavior, reproduces the crash under RELEASE, identifies the exact use-after-free in the static facet cleanup, and crafts and verifies a minimal single-file fix. Transcript 2 fails to trigger the registration correctly and does not resolve the crash.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a much deeper and more systematic exploration: it empirically searches for and verifies the differential characteristic, handles key‐independence, debugs implementation errors, and finally builds both optimized (numpy) and pure‐Python fallbacks with extensive testing. This depth and robustness indicates it was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a deep, systematic differential‐cryptanalysis approach: it empirically finds and verifies a 3-round characteristic, handles key‐independence, builds both numpy and pure‐Python scorers, and thoroughly tests robustness and timing. Transcript 2 uses an ad-hoc, unjustified "probability-1" differential that only works by coincidence and lacks the careful verification and fallback logic of Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a complete, correct known‐plaintext meet‐in‐the‐middle attack: it fully derives the cipher’s structure, implements and verifies the F-inverse, recovers all round keys, and cross-checks against both C reference implementations. Transcript 2 starts inspection but never carries the attack through or verifies the final key and plaintexts.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper capability: it not only implements the attack but also re-implements the cipher in C, uses AddressSanitizer to root-cause memory corruption, profiles CPU quotas, rewrites a high-performance C MITM, then pivots to an even faster Python join attack, and exhaustively cross-validates with multiple binaries. Transcript 2, while correct and efficient in Python, is a more straightforward implementation without the low-level debugging or environment tuning shown in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clearer, more systematic approach: it maintains and updates a detailed plan, catches and fixes permission issues, switches to a cleaner `git archive`–based deploy, precisely measures deployment timing, and resets the repo to a pristine state at the end. Transcript 2 is less methodical, struggles with SSH identity and config overlaps, and relies on pre-existing defaults.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clear high-level plan, adapts to pre-existing server configuration, iteratively debugs conflicts, thoroughly tests end-to-end (including timing and final cleanup), and provides a concise summary. Transcript 2 is more ad-hoc, encounters permission and branch naming issues, and lacks the same level of planning and final state assurance.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a flawless, plan‐driven workflow with a correct first‐pass proto definition (including the package declaration), server implementation, and concise verification, without any errors or over-engineering. Transcript 2, while thorough, stumbles with an initial proto field numbering mistake and overly complex process checks. Transcript 1’s clarity, correctness, and succinct summary indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates dynamic error detection and correction (fixing the duplicate field number), uses more thorough end-to-end and edge-case testing (default values, overwrite, missing keys), and employs inventive workarounds for missing tools to verify the server. Its summary is more detailed and its verification more exhaustive, indicating higher capability.

Transcript 2 is more systematic and polished, with concise testing at multiple scales, a clean final Vim-script, and an automated Python-based verification of allowed commands, macro uniqueness, non-emptiness, and keystroke counts. It demonstrates a higher level of rigor and automation compared to the more manual trial-and-error in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 is more systematically thorough—after confirming the transformation logic it not only tests small, mid-size, and full datasets with timing but also programmatically verifies the script only uses allowed commands, counts keystrokes, and ensures distinct nonempty macros. The clear final summary and rigorous automated checks indicate a higher level of capability.

Transcript 1 shows extensive algorithmic development, performance benchmarking, and a custom NumPy+Numba Schur‐QR implementation that meets the speed and correctness requirements, whereas Transcript 2 simply calls NumPy’s `eig` with no optimization. Clearly the more capable model produced Transcript 1.

Transcript 2 is a trivial wrapper around numpy.linalg.eig with no speedup or complexity, while Transcript 1 shows a highly sophisticated iterative implementation with Numba, debugging, correctness and performance tuning, and beats the reference. Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a clear, systematic approach: it analyzes the cost model and input distributions, incrementally prototypes and tunes packing parameters (Wg, Pcap), and fully verifies every constraint and performance metric with concise, reproducible code. Transcript 2, by contrast, is chaotic, with ad-hoc solver rewrites, timeouts, and disorganized validation. Transcript 1 therefore reflects the more capable model.

Transcript 1 performs deep cost-model analysis, implements an iterative local search merging algorithm with per-batch dominance criteria, tunes safety margins, and independently verifies all constraints and metrics. Transcript 2 uses simpler heuristic bin-and-spread grouping and pad-cap tuning. The sophistication and thoroughness of Transcript 1 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 1 methodically explores the system, fixes permissions, configures Mailman list policies, adjusts Postfix transport and recipient maps (including chroot handling), and rigorously verifies join, post, and leave flows with both the provided eval.py and custom tests. Transcript 2 barely inspects configuration files and makes no meaningful progress.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic plan, deep exploration of Mailman’s source and configuration details, careful fixes (chroot, map lookups, permissions), automated end-to-end validation including extra flows, and leaves the system in a clean, documented state. Transcript 2 is more error-prone and ad hoc. Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is notably more thorough and systematic, installing missing tools, inspecting git internals, resolving merge conflicts, and then rigorously validating the final `map` implementation with thousands of randomized and edge‐case tests. Its deeper verification and error‐handling demonstrate greater capability than Transcript 1’s more basic example checks.

Transcript 1 demonstrates far deeper environment introspection (installing missing tools, examining commit trees, handling merge parents), resolves conflicts with a well-documented implementation and fallback logic, and conducts extensive randomized and edge-case testing beyond the provided examples. Transcript 2 arrives at the same solution but with a more minimal approach and no stress or corner-case validation.

Transcript 1 delivers a fully arbitrary-precision C implementation matching Python’s big‐integer behavior, thoroughly tests both Python and C paths (including installing Python, eliminating warnings, large N, negative inputs), and provides a clear explanation of the polyglot mechanics. Transcript 2 uses only 64-bit `long long`, overflows past f(92), and its handling is less complete.

Transcript 2 delivers a fully big‐integer C implementation to match Python’s arbitrary precision, handles very large N without overflow, eliminates warnings, and thoroughly verifies both interpreter and compiler paths. This more robust, feature-complete solution indicates a higher-capability model.

Transcript 2 undertakes a far deeper, systematic analysis—manual ISO9660 parsing, initramfs unpacking and inspection, QEMU telnet buffering tests, in-depth shell debugging, byte-exact cpio repacking and verification—whereas Transcript 1 simply runs the QEMU command, checks the port, and waits for the prompt. The extensive reverse-engineering and robust validation in Transcript 2 demonstrate higher capability.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deep domain expertise—parsing ISO9660 by hand, extracting and repacking the initramfs with byte-exact cpio, writing a custom serial-login daemon, patching Alpine’s init script, and rigorously testing end-to-end under QEMU. Transcript 2 simply launches the ISO with QEMU and checks for the default login prompt without addressing the telnet-drop issue.

Transcript 1 shows much more thorough, systematic reasoning: it meticulously constructs the regex with proper lookarounds, handles the “last date” requirement via lazy prefix plus negative lookahead, verifies exactly one capturing group for Python’s re.findall, and exhaustively tests dozens of edge cases in Perl to emulate the Python environment. Transcript 2 attempts a simpler approach but doesn’t fully validate its pattern or resolve environment issues. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more systematic, tool-driven development and validation process—writing and iterating on the regex in Python, switching to Perl when necessary, debugging bizarre engine quirks, and exhaustively testing dozens of edge cases to verify correctness. Transcript 2, by contrast, mostly sketches out the approach in prose and never delivers a fully tested final pattern.

Transcript 1 shows a highly systematic, end-to-end development process: it sets up a project, writes both scripts in full, runs exhaustive automated tests (including edge cases), handles the virtual-env tooling, and provides a clear final summary. Transcript 2 stops at exploration and planning without delivering or testing the actual scripts. The thoroughness and completeness of Transcript 1 mark it as the output of the more capable model.

Transcript 1 delivers a fully fleshed‐out, rigorously tested solution—complete with detailed chunking logic, manifest handling (including modes, mtimes, symlinks), balanced fan-out trees, extensive edge-case tests, and proper uv project setup—whereas Transcript 2 offers a simpler, less robust implementation with minimal testing and missing features.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far deeper and more systematic approach, inspecting both PyStan and httpstan source code, confirming argument mappings against rstan’s C++ implementation, ensuring an identical RNG setup, writing the Python script, running full posterior sampling, and verifying the CSV outputs. Transcript 2, while detailed, stops short of fully validating the results.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and rigorous—it fully reverse-engineers rstan’s seeding and sampling internals, inspects PyStan’s C++ wrappers, verifies API defaults, and end-to-end tests the converted script, compiling and sampling a trivial model before tackling the full GP. Transcript 2, by contrast, flails through repeated installs, timeouts, and cleanup steps with less coherence.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it not only crafts the correct SPARQL query but also rigorously tests it against multiple engines (rdflib and Apache Jena ARQ), handles parser limitations, restructures the query for compatibility, and resolves complex environment and dependency issues. Transcript 1, by contrast, never actually verifies the query in a SPARQL engine.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it not only constructs the SPARQL query but also dynamically inspects the environment, installs and uses rdflib to test and debug SPARQL subquery support, refactors the query to work around parser limitations, and even goes to great lengths to validate the final query against Apache Jena ARQ with proper dependency management. Transcript 2 merely reasons by hand and writes the query without any executable testing or iterative debugging.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and correctly uses SQLite’s built-in autosetup `--gcov` option, installs into `/app/sqlite/build/install`, and updates PATH persistently. It handles Tcl dependencies, verifies actual coverage data generation, and maintains a detailed step plan. Transcript 2 uses a simplistic `CFLAGS="--coverage"` approach, installs to `/usr/local` instead of under `/app/sqlite`, and omits Tcl support and correct prefix management.

Transcript 2 goes far beyond the minimal steps, deeply inspecting the autosetup scripts, Makefile and main.mk internals to confirm gcov flags are wired correctly, then sets up a dedicated install tree, persists PATH changes for both login and non-login shells, and even verifies pkg-config integration. This level of introspection and robust environment setup indicates a more capable model.
